outline.rationale: The user is a total beginner who wants hands-on ability to build and train models, and is assumed to have basic Python comfort. Node 1 covers the essential conceptual foundation (what a model/training is) since they have zero background, but stays lightweight. Node 2 gets them set up with the standard practical toolkit without becoming a programming course. Nodes 3–4 form the core build-and-train workflow they explicitly want. Node 5 gives the practical decision-making of picking algorithms for problem types. Node 6 covers evaluation, which is critical to knowing if a model actually works. Node 7 covers iterative improvement (features + hyperparameters) as the natural next step once a baseline model runs. I excluded deep learning architectures, heavy math, deployment at scale, and field history per the confirmed understanding. Ordering follows real dependencies: concepts → tools → data → first model → algorithm choice → evaluation → tuning.
